opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing is that we finally have a way to bring prior knowledge into robotic systems at scale. For a long time in robotics, every time you wanted a robot to do something, you more or less had to start from scratch. You'd collect data for that particular task, in that particular environment, and train a policy that was good at exactly that one thing. And it would be quite brittle: change the lighting, move the table, give it a slightly different object, and it falls apart.

What's changed with large pretrained models, especially vision-language models, is that they've absorbed an enormous amount of knowledge about the world from internet-scale data. They know what objects are, how people talk about tasks, what a reasonable sequence of steps looks like for making a sandwich or folding laundry. They have a kind of common sense that robots never had before. So when we build vision-language-action models on top of them, the robot doesn't have to learn everything from its own experience. It inherits a semantic understanding of the world, and then the robot data teaches it how to ground that understanding in physical action.

The other piece, which I think is just as important, is the recipe itself: the idea that you can train one big generalist model on lots of diverse data from many robots and many tasks, and it actually gets better than specialists. That's the lesson language modeling taught us, and it turns out it transfers to robotics. Data from folding shirts helps with clearing a table; data from one robot helps another with a completely different body. That kind of positive transfer is what lets you imagine scaling robotics the way we scaled language.

Now, I'd be careful not to overstate it. Pretrained models don't solve the physical part. They don't know how hard to grip something, or how to recover when a towel slips. That still has to come from embodied experience, and I think a lot of the exciting work right now is figuring out how robots can get that experience efficiently, including learning from their own deployment and improving with reinforcement learning. But the foundation models give us the scaffolding to build on, and that's a qualitatively different starting point than we had even five years ago.

r001.rationale: The candidate identifies bringing prior knowledge into robotic systems at scale as the biggest benefit of recent AI innovations.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest thing is that we finally have a plausible recipe for generalization. For most of the history of robotics, the bottleneck wasn't really the control problem in a narrow sense. We could get a robot to do one task in one environment with enough engineering. The problem was that the moment you changed the lighting, or the object, or the table, everything fell apart. And robotics didn't have a way to get past that, because you can't hand-engineer your way to a system that handles the open world.

What large models have shown, first in language and then in vision, is that if you train on enough diverse data with a sufficiently general architecture, you get systems that actually transfer. They pick up on the underlying structure of the world rather than memorizing the specifics of their training set. And that's exactly the property robotics has been missing. So when we build something like a vision-language-action model, we're essentially borrowing all of that prior knowledge about what objects are, how scenes are laid out, what instructions mean, and then grounding it in physical actions. The robot doesn't have to learn from scratch what a cup is or that cups usually sit on tables. It inherits that.

The second benefit, which I think is underappreciated, is that it changes the kind of data that's useful. Before, every robotics lab collected its own data for its own robot and its own task, and none of it added up to anything. Now there's a real argument that data pools. Demonstrations from different robots, different labs, different embodiments can all contribute to one model, and even internet-scale data that has nothing to do with robots helps. That turns robotics from a collection of isolated projects into something that can actually accumulate, the way language modeling did.

I'd add one caveat, which is that the physical world is still harder than text. You can't just scrape it. The data has to be collected by robots actually doing things, and that's slow and expensive. So the recipe is there, but the flywheel is still spinning up. But for the first time I think the path is legible. We know roughly what to do, and the question is mostly about scale and about getting robots out into the world so they can generate the experience they need.

r001.rationale: The response says vision-language-action models borrow prior knowledge from language and vision and that robots inherit it, identifying this as a benefit for robotics.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest benefit is the possibility of generalization. Traditionally, when we build a robot that does something well, a lot of the work goes into making it work for that particular task in that particular environment. And if you change the environment, or you ask it to do something slightly different, you might have to do a lot of that work over again.

What we’re seeing with large models is that a single model can acquire knowledge from many different tasks and then use that knowledge to handle a new situation. That’s tremendously valuable for robotics, because the real world has so much variation. You don’t want to have to program every possible way a cup could be sitting on a table.

There’s also an opportunity to bring knowledge from language and images into the robot. A model might already know what a kitchen is and what people typically do there. The hard part is connecting that knowledge to physical action. Knowing how to describe picking up a cup is different from being able to pick it up. But these advances give us a much better starting point for building robots that can learn broadly and adapt.

r001.rationale: The response names generalization as the biggest benefit and explains that a model uses knowledge acquired across tasks to handle new situations, communicating the ability to leverage prior knowledge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest benefit is that we now have a way to bring a lot of prior knowledge into a robot. Historically, if you wanted a robot to do a particular task, you would build a system for that task, or collect a dataset and train it largely from scratch. And that’s a very difficult proposition, because the robot has to learn so much about the world just to do something seemingly simple.

With large pretrained models, you can start with a system that already knows something about objects, about human activities, about what instructions mean. That doesn’t mean it knows how to control a robot. Knowing what a person picking up a cup looks like is different from knowing which motor commands will let you pick up that cup. But it gives you a much better starting point.

The exciting possibility is that experience from different tasks and different environments can contribute to one system. Then learning a new skill becomes less about building an entirely new capability and more about connecting what the model already knows to physical action.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly calls bringing prior knowledge into a robot the biggest benefit, and explains how pretrained models provide that knowledge.
